text: T-SQL has no array column type at all — you'd model a one-to-many relationship with a separate table. PostgreSQL lets a single column genuinely BE an array. Create table products, with a tags column typed as text bracket-bracket. Insert a row using the ARRAY keyword with bracketed values, or the alternate curly-brace literal syntax — both produce the exact same array.

Once you have an array column, unnest is the function you'll reach for constantly. Select product_id, unnest of tags, as tag, from products — this expands each product's array into one row per tag. It's the bridge from one row with an array, to one row per element, which is usually what you actually want to query or join against.

PostgreSQL has two JSON types. Plain JSON stores an exact text copy, preserving whitespace and key order. JSONB stores a parsed binary representation instead — slightly slower to insert, but faster to query, and critically, indexable. For almost any real application, JSONB is the right choice.

Accessing JSONB uses two different arrows. The single arrow returns JSON, keeping quotes and nesting intact. The double arrow returns plain text, unwrapped. Payload arrow user arrow-arrow name gives you back Alex, as a plain string, not a quoted JSON value.

The at-sign greater-than operator tests containment — does this JSONB value contain that one. Where payload contains type colon login. Pair this with a GIN index, and containment queries like this one become genuinely fast, even over large tables.

This is genuinely more capable than T-SQL's JSON support, which treats JSON as text with functions layered on top, rather than a true native, indexable type. Next lesson: common table expressions, and a real version-dependent behavior change you need to know about. See you there.
